explanations.explanation: Ahimelech, the priest at Nob, trembles and asks David, “Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?” (1 Samuel 21:1). I can picture it. David walks in, and the shaking priest asks about the empty space behind him. He skips the small talk and goes straight to the question.

Close, but that's not what Ahimelech asks. A few verses later David says he has brought neither his sword nor his weapons, and he asks Ahimelech, the priest at Nob, for a spear or sword (1 Samuel 21:8). What Ahimelech asks about first is the empty space around David: “Why are you alone?” (1 Samuel 21:1).

The text never says how David traveled, so Ahimelech isn't asking about his shoes or his ride. The priest asks, “Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?” (1 Samuel 21:1). He's looking at who's missing, not at how David got there.

Yes, that's what David says. He tells Ahimelech, “The king has given me a mission…” and adds that the king told him no one is to know about it (1 Samuel 21:2). So David gives the priest his reason in one tidy package, like a lid on a cookie jar.

It's true, actually. David says the king gave him a mission, and that no one is to know about the mission on which he is being sent (1 Samuel 21:2). Those are his words to Ahimelech, the priest at Nob. Easy one to second-guess, friend, because secret missions make everybody squint.

Ahimelech says, “There is no common bread on hand, but there is some consecrated bread” (1 Samuel 21:4). Consecrated means set apart as holy. Verse 6 says it was the Bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD. That's not the sort of bread you grab on a lunch run.

Barley bread is a real thing in the Bible. A boy has five barley loaves in John 6:9. But it isn't what Ahimelech has here. The priest says there is no common bread on hand, only consecrated bread (1 Samuel 21:4). So the bread in this verse is set apart as holy, and nobody mentions its grain.

This one is flipped around. Ahimelech says, “There is no common bread on hand…” (1 Samuel 21:4). The only bread he has is consecrated, set apart as holy. I'd have fallen for it too, friend, because common is the word that sticks.

Yes, David tells him they have. His answer is, “Women have indeed been kept from us, as is usual when I set out.” (1 Samuel 21:5). He adds that the bodies of the young men are holy even on common missions. Ahimelech had set one condition, and David says it's met.

It's true, friend. Ahimelech's condition was that the young men had kept themselves from women, and David answers, “Women have indeed been kept from us, as is usual when I set out.” (1 Samuel 21:5). So David says yes, they have. Then the priest gives him the bread.

Right, the text calls him “…the chief shepherd for Saul.” (1 Samuel 21:7). Doeg the Edomite is Saul's top man over the shepherds. Notice he's "…detained before the LORD." at Nob that day, and the text says no more than that.

Yes, Doeg works for Saul, Israel's king, who is the one David fled from. The text says Doeg was “…the chief shepherd for Saul.” (1 Samuel 21:7). So one of Saul's own servants is at Nob that day. I think that's worth noticing, friend.
Abner was Saul's army commander, the son of Ner (1 Samuel 14:50). He isn't mentioned at Nob. The man the text names is Doeg, “…the chief shepherd for Saul.” (1 Samuel 21:7).

Doeg isn't called a soldier. The text gives him a different title: “…the chief shepherd for Saul.” (1 Samuel 21:7). Doeg the Edomite is the head of Saul's shepherds, and that's the job the text names.

Ahimelech is the priest at Nob, the man David is talking to. Doeg the Edomite is someone else, and the text says he is “…the chief shepherd for Saul.” (1 Samuel 21:7). So the other name goes in the second blank. Two names, two different jobs, friend.

David asks, “Is there not a spear or sword on hand here?” (1 Samuel 21:8). He says he brought neither his sword nor his weapons, because the king's mission was urgent. First bread, now a weapon. Friend, that's a man asking for supplies one question at a time.
David doesn't ask for a horse or a guide. His request is, “Is there not a spear or sword on hand here?” (1 Samuel 21:8). He says he left his weapons behind because the king's mission was urgent.
A cloak and sandals? Friend, David isn't asking for an outfit. He asks, “Is there not a spear or sword on hand here?” (1 Samuel 21:8). He says he brought neither his sword nor his weapons.

Yes, Goliath. Ahimelech says, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here…” (1 Samuel 21:9). It's wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. David killed the man, and now his sword is sitting there wrapped up like a keepsake.

Lahmi was a brother of Goliath the Gittite (1 Chronicles 20:5), but he isn't the man here. Ahimelech names “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah…” (1 Samuel 21:9). It's wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod.

Phicol was the commander of Abimelech's army (Genesis 21:22), which is a whole other story. The sword at Nob belonged to Goliath. Ahimelech says, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here…” (1 Samuel 21:9).

David doesn't turn it down. When Ahimelech says he may take Goliath's sword, David answers, “There is none like it; give it to me.” (1 Samuel 21:9). Ahimelech also says there is no other sword there but this one. So the one sword on hand is the one David asks for.

Right, he takes it. David says, “There is none like it; give it to me.” (1 Samuel 21:9). Ahimelech had told him that no other sword was there but this one. I think David isn't wasting a second on that one.

That day David “…fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath.” (1 Samuel 21:10). Gath was a Philistine city, and Goliath the Philistine had come from Gath (1 Samuel 17:4). So David has the sword of Goliath, and he's walking into the giant's hometown. Friend, that's one bold detour.

Jonathan, Saul's son and David's friend (1 Samuel 20:42), isn't where David goes this time. The text says David “…fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath.” (1 Samuel 21:10). The scene at Nob ends, and the next one is in Gath.

Samuel the prophet did take David in at Ramah once (1 Samuel 19:18), but that isn't this trip. This time David “…fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath.” (1 Samuel 21:10). He's heading for a Philistine king.

explanations.answer: Saul killed thousands and David tens of thousands
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The servants of Achish say, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands…” (1 Samuel 21:11). They remember it as a song sung in their dances. Imagine your hit single coming back at you in Gath, friend.

explanations.answer: David the shepherd fought a lion and a bear
explanations.explanation: David did say he killed both a lion and a bear while keeping his father's sheep (1 Samuel 17:34-36). But that's not the song. The servants of Achish quote this one: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands…” (1 Samuel 21:11).

explanations.answer: David the harpist calmed the troubled king
explanations.explanation: David did play the harp for Saul, and Saul felt relief (1 Samuel 16:23). That isn't in the song the servants remember, though. Theirs goes, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands…” (1 Samuel 21:11). It's all about the battles.
Yes. David “…changed his behavior before them and feigned madness in their hands…” (1 Samuel 21:13). He's very much afraid of Achish, so he pretends to be insane. I think it was a big risk.
The text doesn't show David begging. It says he “…changed his behavior before them and feigned madness in their hands…” (1 Samuel 21:13). He chose to pretend to be insane.

The text doesn't say David slips out through the gate. It says he “…scratched on the doors of the gate…” while he feigned madness (1 Samuel 21:13). So what the text shows at the gate is David acting mad.

explanations.answer: The man is insane so why bring him
explanations.explanation: Yes, Achish tells his servants, “Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me?” (1 Samuel 21:14). He goes on, “Must this man come into my house?” (1 Samuel 21:15). So the act is working. I think Achish sounds more annoyed than alarmed.

explanations.answer: Put this man in chains right now
explanations.explanation: No chains in this scene. Achish says, “Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me?” (1 Samuel 21:14). He's asking his servants why they brought David in at all.

explanations.answer: Send this man back to King Saul
explanations.explanation: Achish never mentions sending David back to Saul, the king of Israel. His words are, “Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me?” (1 Samuel 21:14). He's scolding his own servants, friend.
